summary: TerraPulse is an interactive 3D story that teaches anyone to read NISAR radar data by playing with it. Visitors fly from a globe into Cambodia's Tonle Sap lake, fire radar pulses through monsoon clouds, find Angkor Wat's moat, watch the lake flood real villages one satellite pass at a time, and uncover water hidden under forests that only L-band radar can see. It helps students, journalists and flood planners turn grey decibel images into clear answers: where the water went, when, how much and why. It runs in any browser and converts any NISAR GCOV download into the same explorer.
details:
The challenge it answers

NISAR sees through cloud, day and night, which is exactly when floods happen. But its products are grainy backscatter images in decibels that most people can't read. TerraPulse bridges that gap between powerful data and public understanding.

How it works

A narrated story in five chapters, each teaching one radar concept by doing it: (1) Radar brings its own light: fire pulses that burn through clouds. (2) Dark means water, bright means stone: a warmer/colder game to find Angkor Wat's 190 m moat. (3) Change over time: play a season of 12-day passes while a NISAR model flies over and paints each acquisition, with a live water-area counter in km² and a cross-section on real terrain that shows why a few metres of rise floods kilometres of flat land. (4) L-band's unique ability: sweep a lens over green forest to reveal flooded forest through the double-bounce effect. (5) Free exploration of HH, HV, colour composite, change and elevation layers.

Real 3D context: Copernicus GLO-30 terrain (trees and buildings filtered out to approximate bare ground), a Sentinel-2 base map, and 37,103 OpenStreetMap buildings. Each building checks the radar water flag beneath it, so flooded houses fill with water to the local flood depth.

Trust built in: every visual has a colour bar with units. Hovering or clicking any point shows HH/HV in dB, ground height, water depth, coordinates and the source product. Simplified diagrams, height exaggeration and simulated parts are all labelled on screen.

A real NISAR pipeline: a Python converter reads NISAR L2 GCOV GeoTIFFs and checks that every date shares the same grid. It averages pixels in linear power, flags open water (Otsu threshold) and flooded vegetation (HH double-bounce rule), and exports web layers. On real NISAR data over Sylhet, Bangladesh (5 passes, Aug–Nov 2026), it found and corrected a ~1.5 dB brightness jump between processing versions P05023 and P05036, normalising against stable bright targets.

Accessible: no install, hosted on GitHub Pages, narrated with captions, works on desktop and mobile.

Tools: three.js r160 and custom WebGL shaders (no build step), Python (NumPy, tifffile, imagecodecs), GitHub Pages.

What we'd build next

Convert real NISAR passes over Tonle Sap; validate radar-derived lake levels against Mekong River Commission gauges; add a site picker for any region; add rainfall context from GPM IMERG; add classroom lesson modes; add alerts when a chosen village floods.
